messages.author: 89df6cb36c324fe3
messages.subject: Cumulative probit regression in nimble
parts:
Dear all,

I have been playing around recently with nimble (awesome package!) and was trying fit a kind of cumulative probit type model using it.  However when I tried the following code below (with attached example data), the model did not compile. 

library(nimble)
load("test.RData")

nimmod <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:n) {
    u[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)
    prob[i,1] <- phi(alpha[1]-u[i])
    for(k in 2:(no.levels-1)) { prob[i,k] <- phi(alpha[k]-u[i]) - phi(alpha[k-1]-u[i]) }
    prob[i,no.levels] <- 1-phi(alpha[no.levels-1]-u[i])
    x[i] ~ dcat(prob[i,1:no.levels])
    y[i] ~ dnorm(beta0 + u[i]*beta1, phi)
  }
  
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0,0.0001)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0,0.0001)
  phi <- pow(sigma2, -1)
  sigma2 ~ dunif(0, 100)
  for(k in 1:(no.levels-1)) { alpha0[k] ~ dnorm(0,0.0001) }
  alpha[1:(no.levels-1)] <- sort(alpha0) 
})


nim.params <- c("beta0","beta1","sigma2","u", "alpha")
nim.constants <- list(n = n, no.levels = length(unique(x)))
nim.data <- list(x = x, y = y, n = n, no.levels = length(unique(x)))

nimfit <- nimbleModel(code = nimmod, name = 'madness', constants = nim.constants, data = nim.data)

and produced an error
defining model...
Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(code, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames) : 
  R function 'sort' has arguments that cannot be evaluated; either the function must be a nimbleFunction or values for the following inputs must be specified as constants in the model: alpha0.

Could you please let me know how I can get around the problem with sort? The model as is runs in JAGS without hiccups (provided you give it some starting values for alpha0).

Thanks heaps.

Regards, 
FH

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Cumulative probit regression in nimble
parts:
Hi Francis,

sort() is a JAGS function that we never have gotten around to
implementing in NIMBLE (see Table 5.4 of the User Manual).

One option would be for you to write a user-defined nimbleFunction
that implements sorting and then simply use it in your BUGS code.
Of course sorting is a standard computer science/algorithms problem,
and there is lots of work on efficient ways to do it, but for sorting
a small vector like yours, something basic will probably be fine and
not the bottleneck in your computation.

chris
